en: When the Chinese seized
Aykozho's Bilerik,
You fought without rest for six months
And brought her back, brave Koshoy.
For the paradise that had been sealed,
You became a source of aid, brave Koshoy.
At my noble father's memorial feast,
Be my support, brave Koshoy.
The red banner with its golden finial—
Raise it for me, brave Koshoy.
To my lion father's memorial feast,
Go for me, brave Koshoy.
Let your white beard stream,
And wave it there, brave Koshoy.
Infidels and Muslims
Will crowd there in multitudes;
You have gone forth sowing havoc—
Go for me, brave Koshoy.
Accept these words of mine;
Go and oversee the feast.
Bloodthirsty Manas the leopard
Does not count me equal to his boot heel;
He too is a resounding saint of yours.
I will not go to your Manas;
I will not seek his counsel.
Apart from you,
Even if I die, I will heed no one.
I will not go to overbearing Manas
To say I will hold the feast;
If I die, then let me die,
But I will not heed Manas's words.
I will make Kökötöy's feast spread like a lake;
Kökötöy's great wealth
I will make multiply like spring grass.
I have broad Samarkand and Alay;
If I tell it, I have wealth in plenty.
I have sheep filling the four directions;
If all the eighteen thousand worlds
Come crowding together,
I mean to feed them full.
On this side lies the Syr River;
I have camels filling all of it.
To herd the camels there,
I have giants in abundance;
To lead and distribute the camels,
I have many servants on foot.
For every camel set aside,
I have herds of horses worth
Nine hills of grazing.
I will gather this people in surging crowds;
Mountain-like Koshoy, hear me.
I have the knowledge to load the baggage;
I have gold coins to load on the wise.
My wealth is inexhaustible;
My breast holds many sorrows.
To bring in firewood,
I have many mighty wrestlers.
For the Black Kalmyks and Manchus,
I will make a whole ox their slaughter beast.
The Kalmyks who come teeming,
I will subdue with frozen meat.
People will come in abundance;
A surging flood will come.
Calling it the brow of the great gathering,
Calling it Khan Kökötöy's memorial feast—
Crowding until there is no room on earth,
Let them not end up beneath the earth,
Starting quarrels and causing turmoil,
Shouting as they run about with nowhere to stay,
Screaming as they quarrel.
Take full account of it,
My dear uncle;
Find a spacious place.
If an army spreads across the land,
May there be ample firewood to burn
For the boys who serve them.
When the cauldrons come to the boil,
May steam hide the ground;
So the people do not go thirsty,
May there be a thousand springs of water.
May the place where we hold the feast
Be level ground with a river valley,
And its country broad and wide.
I will entertain the people;
If wrestlers step forth,
Let them seize each other by the cuffs,
Tear whatever flesh they can reach,
And butt like blue bulls.
If heroes ride out to joust,
Let their lances bend.
When the people have gathered
And watch in a circle,
May their fortune be complete;
May it be so broad no dust rises.
If we place Khan Koshoy at the head
And hold Kökötöy's memorial feast,
That is my great desire,”
Bokmurun said, and fell silent.
My elder uncle Koshoy—
A saint who untied the knots
Of ten thousand tangled words,
An elder who became judge of the Katagan,
Dear holy Koshoy.
His white beard gleaming,
Honking like a young goose,
He gathered force and spoke firmly,
Speaking truth without falsehood:
“If we camp in Alay and hold the feast,
And send six swift horses
With a palm-sized letter,
If we strike a Koroson fire-steel
And invite every one,
Infidel and Muslim alike,
When word spreads and the people come,
When a flood comes covering the land
And the people seethe and sway,
Unable to cook and serve the food,
If they hurriedly search for firewood,
And demanding guests beat
All the servants,
What would become of us?
Men whose languages we do not know will come;
From their multitude the black earth
Will barely bear them and will sway.
Those who come making demands
Will recline, calling the feast their due;
All the servants
Will carry dung upon their backs.
Your Alay has no surplus firewood;
That will be a great hardship.”
Your uncle Koshoy went through
All the celebrated places.
“Your celebrated land is Sary-Arka;
Let me tell you its condition.
It has no hill as small as an ankle bone,
No hollow where a saddle blanket could sink.
It has no reed marked by a plow,
No burrow dug by a marmot.
A crow grows old before it can cross;
When a black vulture flies,
By the time it reaches the very center,
Its wings tire and grow weary.
Your Sary-Arka is a waterless desert;
If the people gather in crowds—
Dust will fly in the wind.
Dust clouds will stream and billow;
The people who have gathered
Will shout, unable to find water—
Would that not be utter hardship?
If we go to Suusamyr,
The land on both sides is narrow;
The points of spears will clash,
And people's heads will knock together.
The people will not fit;
They will stand and quarrel with darkened brows.
Its slopes are steep, with no open ground;
The confined land of Suusamyr
Has nowhere to race horses.
The people will crowd without fitting;
It will become a wretched affair,
The uproar deafening the ears.
The people will seethe in crowds;
Your multitude, unable to fit,
Will throng in disorder.
May a black day not befall them
As they steal fire-steels and knives.
I have seen many lands,
Wearing down my horse's flanks,
Roaming and traveling
Around the whole wide world.
There is a place named Karkyra;
That land surpasses all others.
There is no pit to stumble into,
No bank eaten away by water,
No stone to crack a shin.
From every ravine, roaring,
A thousand springs pour down.
In the hollow of Ükürchü,
Along Üch-Kapkak,
There is ground for digging hearth pits;
The broad valley of the Kegen River
Has space along it to race horses
And room to hold great festivities.
The valley of Üch-Karkyra—
That is the place to hold the feast.
Bokmurun, if you heed my words, we shall see
The lances bend
When heroes joust there;
Infidels and Muslims alike
Will gaze in amazement.
There the festivities will be held.”
Dear Koshoy at their head,
Those were the words he spoke.
Koshoy went, and I went;
That was when I stood watching.
Koshoy went, and I went—
Alas, my friend Chynkozho,
When did you ever go with us?
Having heard the elder's words,
Khan's son Bokmurun,
Hearing that Karkyra was good,
Hearing a discerning man's account,
The nobleman's son Bokmurun
Heard that bountiful Karkyra
Was an exceedingly fine summer pasture.
He heard its grazing livestock grew fat,
And that Karkyra, the place for his feast,
Had every blessing in full.
Kökötöy's son Bokmurun
Issued a decree to the Kyrgyz in Tashkent,
Gathering his strength,
And whoever refused to heed him—
He put each household in proper order,
The fires of the teeming multitude
He had extinguished,
And moved them all together.
He had the ornate gray yurts'
Wall frames and roof poles folded,
And loaded them on red camels.
They dismantled the yurts without straying,
And crossed the water without delay;
They drew the red camels' tails
Diagonally up the slope.
Calling it Khan Kökötöy's migration,
He made all the people
See its splendor.
Kökötöy's great wealth
He had loaded on countless gelded camels.
He arrayed them all in splendor
And covered them with robes of honor.
He dressed the graceful girls
In red robes,
Letting the hems of their red robes
Trail diagonally upon the ground,
And Kökötöy's son Bokmurun
Made his prowess known.
He dressed the brides in kete cloth,
Letting the hems of their kete coats
Spread wide and touch the ground,
And Kökötöy's son Bokmurun
Made his generosity known to the people.
He had the swift horse Maaniker
Tethered beneath a rich caparison.
He opened up forty rooms of yellow gold
And spread it all on display.
He had all that gold
Folded into great bundles
And loaded on yellow gelded camels.
He extinguished the fires lit
By the Kyrgyz of Tashkent
And moved them all together.
He raised skyward
The red banner with its golden finial;
Infidels and Muslims alike,
Toward the frontier at Karkyra,
He set them heading for Karkyra.
